html:
Your phone unlocks when it sees your face, YouTube guesses the next video you will enjoy, and a chatbot can write a poem in Nepali in seconds. These are artificial intelligence (AI) at work.

This unit explains how machines learn from data, how robots sense and act, how generative AI writes text and makes pictures, and the ethical questions these tools raise.

It then covers the other technologies changing daily life in Nepal: the Internet of Things, virtual and augmented reality, cloud computing, and online shopping, government services and learning.

What the SEE asks from this unit (11 marks)

The SEE specification grid gives this unit 11 marks: one MCQ (1 mark), three short questions (3 × 2 = 6 marks) and one long question (4 marks) — so most of the marks are written answers.

Typical short questions: define supervised and unsupervised learning, two ethical problems of an AI system, two IoT applications for a given problem, two differences between Internet-based services.

Typical long questions: four guidelines for using AI responsibly, applications of AI or ML, cloud service models, or the merits and limitations of e-commerce, e-governance or e-education.

Most questions are scenarios; answer with points that apply to the situation given, one mark per point.

5.1 Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: meaning, types and applications

Artificial intelligence and machine learning

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science that builds machines able to do tasks that normally need human intelligence: learning, reasoning, solving problems, understanding language, recognising images and making decisions.

Machine learning (ML) is the part of AI in which a computer learns from data and improves with experience, instead of being given step-by-step rules for every case.

The term "artificial intelligence" was coined by John McCarthy for a workshop at Dartmouth College in 1956, and Arthur Samuel named "machine learning" in 1959. Older programs followed only the rules a programmer wrote.

To teach a computer to tell a cat from a dog with rules you would need endless instructions about ears and whiskers; with machine learning you show it thousands of labelled photos and it works out the difference itself.

Deep learning is machine learning that uses large networks of simple units (neural networks), and generative AI is deep learning that creates new content.

Artificial intelligence Machine learning
the broad field of making machines think and act intelligently a subset of AI that makes machines learn from data
uses reasoning, rules, search, language processing and learning uses data, patterns and predictions
may follow fixed rules or learn always learns from examples
examples: hotel service robots, chatbots, smart assistants examples: spam filters, YouTube recommendations, fraud alerts

Types of AI

By capability Meaning Exists?
Narrow (weak) AI very good at one task — translation, face unlock, chess, chat yes: every AI in use today
General (strong) AI could learn any intellectual task a human can not yet; a research goal
Super AI would be more intelligent than humans in every field only an idea

AI can also be grouped by how it works: reactive machines respond to the present only (IBM's Deep Blue, which beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997); limited-memory AI uses recent data and experience (self-driving cars, chatbots — almost all modern AI); theory-of-mind and self-aware AI, which would understand feelings or itself, do not exist.

Applications of AI and ML

Area What AI does Example
Gaming plans moves and plays against humans chess and football games, computer opponents
Natural language processing (NLP) understands and produces human language Google Translate between Nepali and English, Siri, Alexa
Automated grading checks and scores answers instantly Google Forms quizzes, Grammarly, Quillionz
Personalised learning adapts lessons to each learner Duolingo
Expert systems gives advice using stored expert knowledge helping doctors diagnose diseases
Computer vision recognises faces and objects in images face lock, number-plate reading
Handwriting recognition turns handwriting into editable text scanning notes with a phone
Intelligent robots sense, decide and act factory, hospital and space robots

Machine learning in particular powers email spam detection, speech recognition (voice typing), image recognition, self-driving cars, chatbots and virtual assistants, fraud detection in banks and wallets (an unusual payment from a new phone is flagged), social-media feeds that show what you are likely to watch, monitoring of the dark web for crime, and cybersecurity systems that spot attacks such as phishing.

Worked example 5.1 — AI, ML or neither?

Problem. Classify each:(a) a calculator adding 245 + 378;(b) Daraz showing "customers also bought";(c) a chess program that searches millions of moves with fixed rules;(d) a phone camera recognising a face it has learnt.

Solution.(a) Neither — it follows fixed arithmetic rules and shows no intelligence.(b) ML — it learns buying patterns from millions of orders.(c) AI but not ML — it reasons and plans, but with rules written by people.(d) ML (deep learning) — it learnt the face from examples.

Activity 1 — a table of AI tools

In groups, list five recent AI tools for mobile and desktop with the developer, key features and an application, and present them. For example:

AI tool Developer Key features Application
ChatGPT OpenAI conversation, writing, coding help, image input explaining a topic, drafting
Gemini Google chat, built into Gmail and Docs summarising, writing help
Microsoft Copilot Microsoft chat; works inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint drafting and data analysis
Google Translate Google text, voice and camera translation, including Nepali understanding signs and notices
Grammarly Grammarly Inc. grammar, spelling and tone suggestions correcting essays and emails

Key applications of AI

  1. Education. AI tutors answer a student's questions at any hour and set practice questions at the right level. Translation tools help students read English books in Nepali. Teachers use AI to mark multiple-choice tests quickly.
  2. Healthcare. AI reads X-ray and retina images and warns the doctor of a possible disease. In a hill district a health worker can send a picture to a hospital model for a first opinion. This saves time where specialists are few.
  3. Agriculture. A phone app can recognise a leaf disease from a photograph and suggest a remedy. Models predict rainfall and the best time for planting. Farmers of Nepal can reduce losses.
  4. Banking and finance. AI spots unusual transactions on a card or wallet and blocks fraud. Credit models decide the risk of a loan. Chatbots answer customers' questions on the mobile-banking app.
  5. Transport. Navigation apps predict traffic in Kathmandu and suggest quicker roads. Self-driving cars use cameras and AI to detect lanes and people. Ride-sharing apps match drivers with passengers.
  6. Entertainment and social media. Music and video apps suggest songs and clips that match your taste. Filters and face tags use image recognition. Game characters use AI to decide their moves.
  7. Security and surveillance. Face recognition opens a phone and checks identity at an airport. Cameras detect an intruder and send an alert. This must be used with care for privacy.
  8. Language and voice assistants. Voice assistants such as Google Assistant understand speech and answer. Speech-to-text writes subtitles, and chatbots such as ChatGPT write text and code. Nepali voice support is growing.

5.2 Learning techniques: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning

A machine learns by finding patterns in data. How it is taught gives three main learning techniques.

The three learning techniques
  • Supervised learning: the machine is trained on labelled data — every example comes with the correct answer (the label) — and learns to predict the label of new examples. It is like learning with a teacher who gives the answers.
  • Unsupervised learning: the machine gets unlabelled data and must find patterns or groups by itself (clustering). It is like exploring materials with no teacher.
  • Reinforcement learning: an agent learns by trial and error: it acts in an environment, receives a reward for good actions and a penalty for bad ones, and gradually learns the actions that earn the most reward.
There are three main techniques, not two

Alongside supervised and unsupervised learning, machine learning also includes reinforcement learning, which is how game-playing programs such as AlphaGo and many robots learn.

(Semi-supervised learning, which mixes a few labelled examples with many unlabelled ones, is a fourth, less common type.)

Point Supervised Unsupervised Reinforcement
Data labelled (with answers) unlabelled no fixed data; experience from actions
Goal predict the label of new data find groups or patterns find the actions that earn most reward
Feedback the correct answer for every example none reward or penalty after actions
Like learning… with a teacher who gives answers alone, by exploring by practice, from success and failure
Examples spam or not spam; pass or fail; cat or dog grouping customers by shopping habits a robot learning to walk; a game-playing AI; self-driving practice in simulation
Program 5.1 — a tiny supervised learner in Python

Problem. Eight students' daily study hours and attendance are labelled "pass" or "fail". Predict the result of three new students by looking at the three most similar labelled students (the k-nearest-neighbour method).

Solution.

# Supervised learning: learn "pass" or "fail" from labelled examples
training = [
    # (hours of study per day, attendance %, label)
    (1.0, 60, "fail"), (1.5, 72, "fail"), (2.0, 65, "fail"), (2.5, 80, "pass"),
    (3.0, 85, "pass"), (3.5, 70, "pass"), (4.0, 90, "pass"), (0.5, 85, "fail"),
]

def distance(a, b):
    # attendance is divided by 10 so that both features count about equally
    return ((a[0] - b[0]) ** 2 + ((a[1] - b[1]) / 10) ** 2) ** 0.5

def predict(hours, attendance, k=3):
    nearest = sorted(training, key=lambda row: distance((hours, attendance), row))[:k]
    labels = [row[2] for row in nearest]
    return max(set(labels), key=labels.count)

for student in [(2.8, 78), (1.2, 68), (3.8, 60)]:
    print(student, "->", predict(*student))

(2.8, 78) -> pass
(1.2, 68) -> fail
(3.8, 60) -> pass

The program was never told a rule such as "study 2.5 hours to pass"; it predicts from the labelled examples alone. For (3.8, 60) the three nearest students are pass, fail and pass, so the majority answer is pass.

Worked example 5.2 — which technique?

Problem. Name the learning technique:(a) Gmail learns spam from millions of emails marked "spam" or "not spam";(b) a shop groups its customers by buying habits without any categories given;(c) a computer learns to play a game by winning and losing thousands of times;(d) Teachable Machine learns cats and dogs from photos you label.

Solution.(a) Supervised — labelled examples.(b) Unsupervised — it discovers the groups.(c) Reinforcement — rewards for winning.(d) Supervised — every photo is labelled cat or dog.

Activity 1.2 — train a model with Teachable Machine

Open teachablemachine.withgoogle.com → Get Started → Image Project. Name Class 1 "Cat" and Class 2 "Dog", upload five photos to each, and click Train Model. In Preview test new photos and note the confidence bars.

Then test a photo of a rabbit: the model must still answer "cat" or "dog", because it knows only the labels it was taught — a limit of supervised learning worth discussing in class.

5.3 AI in robotics: sensing, deciding and acting

Robot and robotics

A robot is a programmable machine that senses its surroundings, decides what to do and acts on the world, often without human help. Robotics is the field of designing, building, programming and operating robots.

AI in robotics means using AI — computer vision, speech, learning and planning — so that robots can understand their surroundings and decide for themselves rather than repeat one fixed movement.

Every robot repeats a sense–think–act cycle many times a second:

  • Sense — sensors collect information: cameras, microphones, distance (ultrasonic or infrared) sensors, touch, temperature and light sensors.
  • Think (decide) — the controller (a computer or a microcontroller such as an Arduino) processes the readings and chooses an action, using programmed rules or AI.
  • Act — actuators (motors, wheels, arms, grippers, speakers) carry the action out, which changes what the sensors read next.

Robots are used for jobs that are dangerous, difficult or boring for people: bomb disposal, fire fighting, exploring the ocean floor and other planets (NASA's Mars rovers), work in nuclear or chemical plants, welding and painting in car factories, warehouse picking, robotic surgery (such as the da Vinci system), fruit picking and spraying on farms, and cleaning homes (robot vacuum cleaners).

They make work faster, safer and more accurate.

Simulating simple robotic tasks

Before a real robot is built, its program is tested in a simulator, where a mistake costs nothing.

Activity 1.3 — a robot in Scratch

At scratch.mit.edu, create a project, delete the cat, and choose a robot sprite and a backdrop.

Build: when green flag clicked → say "Starting patrol" for 2 seconds → repeat 4 { move 100 steps → turn ↻ 90 degrees → say "Corner reached" for 1 second }. Click the green flag: the robot walks round a square and speaks at each corner.

(Activity 1.4 does the same in an online robot simulator such as RoboBlocky: four "drive forward" and four "turn 90°" blocks make a perfect square.)

Program 5.2 — a robot that senses an obstacle

Problem. A robot starts at square (0, 0) of a grid and must reach the goal (5, 2). Boxes block squares (3, 0) and (3, 1).

Each turn it senses the square to its east: if it is clear and the robot has not reached the goal's column, it moves east; otherwise it moves north. Simulate it.

Solution.

# A robot on a grid: sense, think, act until it reaches the goal
obstacles = [(3, 0), (3, 1)]       # squares blocked by boxes
goal = (5, 2)
x, y = 0, 0
step = 0
while (x, y) != goal:
    step += 1
    ahead = (x + 1, y)                       # SENSE: look one square east
    if x < goal[0] and ahead not in obstacles:
        x = x + 1                            # THINK: path clear, so ACT: move east
        action = "east"
    else:
        y = y + 1                            # blocked (or column reached): move north
        action = "north"
    print("Step", step, ": moved", action, "to", (x, y))
print("Goal reached in", step, "steps")

Step 1 : moved east to (1, 0)
Step 2 : moved east to (2, 0)
Step 3 : moved north to (2, 1)
Step 4 : moved north to (2, 2)
Step 5 : moved east to (3, 2)
Step 6 : moved east to (4, 2)
Step 7 : moved east to (5, 2)
Goal reached in 7 steps

Each pass of the loop is one sense–think–act cycle; the path is drawn in the figure above.

5.4 Generative AI: how it works, prompting and limitations

Generative AI

Generative AI is AI that creates new content — text, images, music, video or computer code — in response to an instruction called a prompt.

It learns from huge amounts of existing data and then produces original output, so the same prompt can give a different answer each time.

How large language models work

A large language model (LLM), such as the one behind ChatGPT, is a very large neural network trained on an enormous amount of text: books, websites, articles and code.

Text is broken into small pieces called tokens (words or parts of words).

During training the model is shown billions of sentences with the next token hidden and adjusts itself to predict the next token correctly; it is then fine-tuned with human feedback to be helpful and safe.

When you type a prompt, it writes the answer one token at a time: it gives every possible next token a probability, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats.

Most modern LLMs use the transformer design, published by Google researchers in 2017.

An image generator such as DALL·E or Stable Diffusion is usually a diffusion model. It learns from millions of pictures paired with their captions.

To make a picture it starts from random noise and removes the noise step by step, each step guided by the words of your prompt, until an image appears.

Popular generative AI tools

Tool Made by Head of the company (2026) Mainly for
ChatGPT OpenAI (launched November 2022) Sam Altman conversation, writing, coding; reads files and images
Gemini Google DeepMind, Google (Alphabet) Sundar Pichai chat; built into Gmail, Docs and Android
Microsoft Copilot Microsoft, using OpenAI's models Satya Nadella chat; built into Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint
GitHub Copilot GitHub, a Microsoft company (Microsoft) suggesting code while you program
Claude Anthropic Dario Amodei writing, analysis and coding
DeepSeek DeepSeek (China) Liang Wenfeng chat and coding
DALL·E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Adobe Firefly OpenAI, Midjourney, Stability AI, Adobe — making images from text
"Copilot" is more than one product

When distinguishing Copilot tools, note that there are really two: Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft's assistant in Windows and Microsoft 365, and GitHub Copilot, a coding assistant made by GitHub (owned by Microsoft).

Both are built on OpenAI's GPT models, which is where OpenAI comes in.

Prompting

A prompt is the instruction given to a generative AI.

The answer is only as good as the prompt, so a good prompt states the task, gives context (who it is for, what you already know), sets the format and length, adds limits (language, level, what to avoid), and is refined if the first answer is not right.

Worked example 5.3 — improving a prompt

Problem. Improve the prompt "Tell me about IoT."

Solution. A weak prompt gives a long, general answer. A better one: "Explain the Internet of Things to a Class 10 student in Nepal in about 150 words.

Give two examples from agriculture and one from homes, and end with two practice questions." It names the audience, length, examples and format, so the answer fits the need.

If the answer uses hard words, follow up with "Use simpler English."

Limitations of generative AI

  • Hallucination — it can state false facts, invent sources or give wrong calculations in confident language, because it predicts likely words rather than checking facts.
  • Out-of-date knowledge — it knows only what was in its training data unless it is connected to the Internet.
  • Bias — it can repeat unfair stereotypes present in its training data.
  • Privacy — anything you type may be stored; never enter passwords, phone numbers or private documents.
  • Copyright and honesty — submitting AI-written work as your own is cheating, and generated images may copy others' styles.
  • Misuse — fake photos, voices and videos (deepfakes) are used for scams and false news.
Activity 1.5 — make an image from a prompt

Use a free image generator (Microsoft Designer's image creator, Canva's AI image tool or Craiyon). Try "a robot teacher in a classroom in Nepal, cartoon style", then change one word at a time and compare the pictures.

Display your favourite with a one-line caption, and note one thing the generator got wrong.

5.5 Application of integrated AI tools in study and work

AI is now built into the everyday tools of school and office work, so you use it without opening a separate chatbot.

Tool Integrated AI features How they help
Google Docs Smart Compose (suggests the rest of a sentence), spelling and grammar suggestions, voice typing, translation of the whole document, summaries and "Help me write" (Gemini) faster, cleaner writing; dictating in Nepali or English
Gmail Smart Compose and Smart Reply, spam filtering, grammar suggestions, email summaries quicker replies, a cleaner inbox
Microsoft 365 Copilot in Word (drafting and rewriting), Excel (formulas, charts, data analysis), PowerPoint (Designer layouts, slides from a document), Teams (meeting transcripts and recaps) reports, data analysis and presentations in less time
Phones voice assistants, live translation, camera text recognition (Google Lens) reading notices, translating, accessibility

(Gmail's "schedule send" is a timer feature rather than AI, whereas Smart Reply and spam filtering use AI.)

In study, these tools can explain a hard concept in simpler words, make practice questions from your notes, check grammar, translate between Nepali and English, turn speech into text, and summarise a long chapter.

In work, they draft letters and reports, analyse sales data, prepare presentations, record meeting notes and answer customers through chatbots.

Four rules for using AI in schoolwork

Privacy — never enter personal details of yourself or others. Accuracy — verify every important fact and figure against a trusted reference source. Fairness — watch for biased or one-sided answers.

Honesty — use AI to learn and to check your work, not to do it; say when you have used it, and write the final answer in your own words.

5.6 Ethics in AI: bias, privacy and security

Ethics is the set of moral principles that tells us what is right and wrong, fair and unfair.

AI decides who sees which advertisement, which loan is approved and which face matches a criminal record, so it must be fair, safe, private, transparent and accountable.

In August 2025 Nepal's cabinet approved a National Artificial Intelligence Policy, 2082 to promote AI skills and ethical, transparent use of AI.

Bias. An AI system is biased when it treats people unfairly because of gender, caste, ethnicity, language, age or region.

AI learns from past data, so it copies the unfairness in that data: a hiring AI trained mostly on men's CVs may reject women; a face-recognition system trained mostly on light-skinned faces makes more mistakes with darker skin; a speech system trained on one accent may fail for speakers from other regions.

Fixes: train on diverse and representative data, test the results for different groups, and keep a human able to check and overrule decisions.

Privacy. AI collects and analyses huge amounts of personal data — photos, location, messages, health and shopping records. Misused or leaked, it can lead to identity theft, spying, blackmail or unfair treatment.

Data should be collected only with consent, only as much as is needed, stored securely and deleted when no longer needed. Nepal's Individual Privacy Act, 2075 protects personal information.

Security. AI systems can be attacked: hackers may steal their data, change their training data so that they learn wrong behaviour (data poisoning), or fool them with specially altered inputs — stickers on a road sign that make a self-driving car misread "Stop".

AI is also used by criminals for deepfake scams and convincing phishing messages. Protection: encryption, strong passwords and access control, regular testing, and human oversight of important decisions.

Worked example 5.4 — ethical problems in a scenario

Problem. A bank uses an AI system to approve loans automatically from applicants' data. Explain two ethical problems and one safeguard for each.

Solution. (1) Bias: if past loan data favoured men or applicants from cities, the AI will repeat that unfairness — the bank should test approval rates for different groups and train on balanced data.

(2) Privacy and transparency: the system uses sensitive financial data and cannot easily explain its decisions — the bank should collect only necessary data with consent, protect it, explain the reasons for a refusal, and let a human officer review rejected applications.

5.7 Internet of Things (IoT) and its applications

Internet of Things

The Internet of Things (IoT) is the network of everyday physical objects — appliances, vehicles, machines, sensors, wearables — fitted with sensors, software and network connections, so that they collect data, exchange it over the Internet and act on it, often without human intervention.

An IoT system has sensors (measuring temperature, moisture, motion, light, location), a small computer or microcontroller that reads them, a connection (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data), a cloud server that stores and analyses the data, an app where people see it, and actuators that act — switch on a pump, lock a door, turn off a light.

A smoke detector that alerts the fire brigade and the owner's phone by itself is a simple IoT system.

Application What IoT does Example
Smart home lights, fans, plugs, cameras and locks controlled from a phone; automatic switching a smart bulb that turns on at sunset
Smart city traffic lights that adjust to traffic, smart street lights, parking sensors, full-bin alerts, air-quality monitors less congestion and energy waste
Smart agriculture soil-moisture sensors control irrigation; greenhouse temperature monitoring; livestock trackers water given only when the crop needs it
Smart healthcare wearables measure heartbeat and steps; remote monitoring of patients an elderly patient's readings sent to the doctor
Smart transportation GPS tracking of buses and taxis, ride-hailing apps, smart toll and fuel cards seeing exactly where the bus is
Smart education RFID or fingerprint attendance, smart boards, connected labs attendance recorded automatically
Communication and industry machines report faults before breaking down; stock tracked with RFID maintenance done in time

IoT saves time, energy and money and gives accurate, real-time information. Its challenges are security (badly protected devices are easy to hack), privacy (devices collect personal data), dependence on the Internet and electricity, cost, and electronic waste.

Key applications of IoT

  1. Smart homes. Lights, fans and door locks are switched from a phone, and a motion sensor turns on the light when someone enters. This saves electricity and adds comfort.
  2. Smart agriculture. Soil-moisture sensors tell a farmer when to water, and an automatic pump starts by itself. Water is saved and the crop grows better.
  3. Healthcare. A wearable band measures heart rate and sends it to the doctor. Elderly patients are monitored from far away.
  4. Smart metering. A smart meter reports the electricity used, so the bill is correct without a meter reader. The Nepal Electricity Authority is introducing such meters.
  5. Transport and tracking. GPS trackers show the position of a bus or a delivery bike on a map. Fleet owners save fuel and customers know when the vehicle will arrive.
  6. Industry. Sensors on a machine detect heat or vibration and warn before it breaks, which prevents costly stoppage.
  7. Environment and disaster warning. River-level and rainfall sensors send alerts of floods to villages. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology uses such stations.
  8. Smart cities. Street lights dim when no one is passing, bins signal when full and parking sensors guide drivers to a free place.

5.8 Virtual reality, augmented reality and extended reality (XR)

VR, AR and XR

Virtual reality (VR) is a completely computer-generated 3D environment that feels real; a headset covers the eyes and the view changes as the head moves.

Augmented reality (AR) adds digital images or information on top of the real world, seen through a phone camera or special glasses. Mixed reality (MR) goes further, letting digital objects interact with real ones.

Extended reality (XR) is the umbrella term for all of them.

Point Virtual reality (VR) Augmented reality (AR) Mixed reality (MR)
What you see only a computer-made world the real world with digital additions real world and digital objects that interact
Device VR headset (e.g. Meta Quest) smartphone, tablet, AR glasses MR headset (e.g. Microsoft HoloLens)
Contact with the real world cut off kept kept
Examples VR games, virtual tours, flight simulators Pokémon GO, Google Lens translating a sign, camera filters, seeing furniture in your room before buying engineers handling a 3D model on a real table

Applications of VR and XR: education (virtual field trips, 3D models of the heart or the solar system), training (pilots, drivers, surgeons and soldiers practise safely), health (therapy and rehearsing operations), business (virtual showrooms and property tours), entertainment (games, concerts, films), military and defence, tourism and hospitality (previewing hotels and heritage sites), and aeronautics (flight simulators and aircraft design).

5.9 Cloud computing: service models and applications

Cloud computing

Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services — servers, storage, databases, software, networking and analytics — over the Internet, on demand, paying only for what is used, instead of buying and maintaining your own hardware and software.

The provider runs the equipment in large data centres.

The largest providers are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud. Everyday cloud apps include Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud, Gmail, Google Docs and Microsoft 365.

Features of cloud computing: on-demand self-service; access from anywhere on any device; scalability (resources grow or shrink as needed); resource pooling (many customers share the provider's machines); pay-as-you-go pricing; and maintenance, updates and backups done by the provider.

Benefits Limitations
no costly servers to buy; pay only for use needs a reliable Internet connection
files available anywhere, any time, on any device data is held by another company: privacy concerns
easy teamwork on shared documents provider outages stop the service
automatic backup and updates monthly costs add up; hard to move to another provider
scales instantly for big events (SEE results day) less control over how the system is run

Service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

Model What the provider gives Who uses it Examples
IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service virtual servers, storage and networks; you install and manage the operating system and software IT teams and system administrators Amazon EC2 and S3, Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine
PaaS — Platform as a Service a ready platform (operating system, runtime, database, tools) to develop, test and run your own applications software developers Google App Engine, Azure App Service, Heroku, Firebase
SaaS — Software as a Service complete applications used through a browser or app; nothing to install or maintain everyone Gmail, Google Docs, Microsoft 365, Zoom, Canva, Google Drive, OneDrive

Google Drive and OneDrive are SaaS, not IaaS

Consumer cloud storage apps such as Google Drive and OneDrive are finished applications used through a browser or app, so they are SaaS.

IaaS means renting raw infrastructure — a virtual server or block of storage that your own IT staff set up and manage, such as Amazon EC2.

Clouds are also described by who can use them: a public cloud is shared by any paying customer (AWS, Google Cloud); a private cloud serves one organisation; a hybrid cloud combines the two.

Worked example 5.5 — which service model?

Problem. Name the model:(a) a school writes its routine in Google Docs;(b) a company rents ten virtual servers from AWS and installs its own software;(c) a student hosts her Python web app on Google App Engine;(d) a teacher designs posters in Canva.

Solution.(a) SaaS.(b) IaaS.(c) PaaS.(d) SaaS.

Activity 1.6 — how does cloud storage work?

Find out how Google Drive or OneDrive keeps your files: where the data centres are, how files are copied to several places for safety, how sharing links and permissions work, and how syncing keeps your phone and laptop copies the same.

Prepare a five-slide presentation for your class.

5.10 e-Commerce, e-Governance and e-Education in Nepal

ICT and the Internet now let people shop, use government services and study without leaving home or standing in long queues.

e-Commerce

e-Commerce

e-Commerce (electronic commerce) is the buying and selling of goods and services, and the payment for them, over the Internet.

In Nepal Daraz and SastoDeal sell goods online, HamroBazar lets people sell to each other, and Foodmandu and Pathao deliver food; digital wallets and payment systems such as eSewa, Khalti, Fonepay QR and connectIPS let buyers pay from their phones.

The types are B2C (business to consumer, e.g. Daraz), C2C (consumer to consumer, e.g. HamroBazar) and B2B (business to business, e.g. a shop ordering stock from a wholesaler online).

Parliament passed the E-Commerce Act, 2081 in 2025, which requires online businesses to register with the government.

Merits of e-commerce Limitations
shop from home, 24 hours a day the product delivered may differ from the picture
saves time and travel online scams and fraud
wide choice, including international products less face-to-face contact
easy price comparison and doorstep delivery dependence on technology and the Internet
digital payment without cash delivery can be late; returns can be slow

e-Governance

e-Governance

e-Governance is the use of digital technology and the Internet by the government to provide services and information to citizens, businesses and its own offices efficiently and transparently.

Type Between Nepali example
G2C — Government to Citizen government and people Nagarik App (linked citizenship, PAN, licence and voter details), online passport application, online SEE and NEB results
G2B — Government to Business government and companies online company registration, tax filing on the Inland Revenue Department's portal, e-bidding for government contracts
G2G — Government to Government between offices shared data between ministries and local governments
G2E — Government to Employee government and its staff online salary and pension records

Nepal's Digital Nepal Framework (2019) set out plans to deliver more services online, and citizens can file complaints through the Hello Sarkar service.

Merits of e-governance Limitations
transparency: citizens can track applications digital divide: not everyone has a device or Internet

e-Education

e-Education

e-Education (e-learning) is the use of digital technology and the Internet for teaching and learning, so that lessons, videos, assignments and exams can be reached from computers, tablets or phones at any time and place.

Examples in Nepal include the government's Sikai Chautari portal (learning.cehrd.gov.np) with lessons and textbooks for Grades 1–10, OLE Nepal's E-Paath lessons and E-Pustakalaya library, and online classes in Google Classroom, Zoom and Google Meet, which schools and colleges used widely during the COVID-19 lockdowns.

Merits of e-education Limitations
learn at your own pace, anytime and anywhere little face-to-face contact with teachers and friends
a huge variety of materials, often free needs devices, electricity and Internet
lessons can be replayed technical problems interrupt learning
often cheaper than travelling to classes quality varies; self-discipline is needed
flexible for working students and remote areas practical subjects are harder to teach online

Chapter summary

  • AI makes machines do tasks needing human intelligence; ML is AI that learns from data; deep learning and generative AI are inside ML. All present AI is narrow AI.
  • Learning techniques: supervised (labelled data, predicts labels), unsupervised (unlabelled data, finds groups), reinforcement (trial and error with rewards).
  • Robots sense (sensors), think (controller, AI) and act (actuators); simulators such as Scratch and RoboBlocky test robot programs.
  • Generative AI creates content from prompts: LLMs predict the next token; image generators remove noise step by step. Good prompts give task, context, format and limits. Limits: hallucination, bias, privacy, copyright, deepfakes.
  • AI is built into Google Docs, Gmail and Microsoft 365 (Copilot); use it with privacy, accuracy, fairness and honesty.
  • AI ethics: bias (fix with diverse data and human review), privacy (consent, minimal data), security (protect against hacking and poisoning).
  • IoT: sensors + connection + cloud + app + actuators, in smart homes, cities, farms, health, transport and schools.
  • VR replaces the real world; AR adds to it; MR mixes them; XR covers all three.
  • Cloud models: IaaS (infrastructure), PaaS (platform), SaaS (software). e-Commerce (Daraz, eSewa), e-governance (Nagarik App, G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E) and e-education (Sikai Chautari) bring services online in Nepal.

Answers to Group B

1. Machine learning is the part of AI in which a computer learns patterns from data and improves with experience instead of being given fixed rules.

Example Gmail's spam filter learning from emails marked spam.

2. Supervised learning trains on labelled data with correct answers; reinforcement learning has no labelled answers and learns by trial and error from rewards and penalties.

Supervised learning predicts labels (spam/not spam); reinforcement learning learns actions (a robot learning to walk).

3. Sense — sensors collect information about the surroundings; think — the controller or AI decides what to do; act — actuators such as motors carry out the action.

4. It can hallucinate (give false facts confidently), so every fact must be checked; and submitting its writing as your own is dishonest, so it should be used to learn, not to do the work (also bias and privacy).

5. Privacy — X-rays and records are sensitive and must be protected and used only with consent. Accuracy and bias — the AI may make mistakes, especially for groups missing from its training data, so a doctor must check its findings.

6. Soil-moisture sensors that switch irrigation pumps on only when the soil is dry, saving water and electricity; weather or pest sensors that send alerts to the farmer's phone, so crops can be protected in time (also livestock trackers).

7. VR replaces the real world with a computer-made one, seen in a headset — e.g. a VR game or virtual tour. AR adds digital information on top of the real world through a phone or glasses — e.g. Google Lens translating a signboard.

8. Benefits: files and software available to teachers and students anywhere; no need to buy and maintain servers; automatic backup. Limitation: it needs a reliable Internet connection.

9. G2C: the Nagarik App or online passport applications (also online results). G2B: online company registration or tax filing on the IRD portal.

Answers to Group C

1. AI is the field of computer science that builds machines able to do tasks needing human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning and recognising images (1).

Supervised learning learns from labelled examples, e.g. a spam filter trained on emails marked spam. Unsupervised learning finds groups in unlabelled data, e.g. grouping customers by buying habits.

Reinforcement learning learns by trial and error from rewards, e.g. a robot learning to walk or a game-playing program (1 each).

2. (1)

Privacy never type personal details, passwords or photos of others into an AI tool. (2)

Accuracy verify every answer against a trusted reference source, because AI can hallucinate. (3)

Fairness and bias notice one-sided or stereotyped answers and question them. (4)

Academic honesty use AI to understand and practise, write the final answer in your own words, and say when AI helped (also safety: use school-approved tools only).

3. Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services such as storage, servers, databases and software over the Internet, on demand and pay-per-use (1).

Model answer D1: AI, machine learning and applications (10 marks)

Introduction. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer or machine to do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as understanding speech, recognising pictures, learning and making decisions.

Machine learning (ML) is a part of AI in which a computer learns patterns from data instead of being given fixed rules.

Types of AI by ability.

  1. Narrow (weak) AI: designed for one task, such as a spam filter or a chess program. All AI used today is of this type.
  2. General (strong) AI: would match a human in any intellectual task. It does not exist yet.
  3. Super AI: would be smarter than all humans; this is only an idea.

Types of machine learning.

Type Data How it learns Example
Supervised Labelled (question and answer) Learns the link between input and the right answer Spam or not spam; price prediction
Unsupervised Unlabelled Finds groups and patterns by itself Grouping customers
Reinforcement None given; feedback Tries actions and gets rewards or penalties A robot learning to walk; a game player

Applications. Education (AI tutors), healthcare (reading X-ray images), agriculture (leaf-disease apps), banking (fraud detection), transport (traffic prediction), entertainment (recommendations), security (face recognition), and voice assistants.

Advantages and limitations. AI works fast, never tires and can find patterns that people miss. But it needs large data and costly hardware, can be biased if the data are biased, can take jobs of routine work, and cannot show real feelings or common sense.

Conclusion. AI is already part of daily life in Nepal, and learning how it works helps students use it wisely.

Model answer D2: generative AI and ethics (10 marks)

Introduction. Generative AI is AI that creates new content, such as text, images, music, code or video, after learning from huge amounts of existing data. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude write text, and image tools draw pictures from a description.

How it works. (1) The model is trained on very large collections of text or images. (2) It learns the patterns, for text mainly which word is likely to come next. (3) The user writes a prompt, an instruction.

(4) The model produces an answer word by word from probabilities. A better prompt gives a better answer: it names the task, gives the context, states the format and the length.

Uses in study and work. Summarising a chapter, explaining a hard idea, preparing practice questions, translating, checking grammar, writing code and drafting a letter or a presentation.

Limitations. It can give wrong facts with confidence (called hallucination); it may be biased; it does not truly understand; its knowledge stops at a training date; it can be used to copy and cheat, and it needs a lot of electricity.

Ethics of AI.

  1. Bias: unfair results when the training data favour one group, such as a hiring tool that prefers men.
  2. Privacy: personal data collected to train or run AI may be misused.
  3. Security: AI can write phishing mails or make fake voices and deepfake videos.
  4. Accountability: who is responsible when an AI decision causes harm?
  5. Jobs: automation may replace routine work.
  6. Honesty: students should not submit AI work as their own.
Benefit Risk
Saves time Wrong answers believed
Personal tutor Cheating
Creative help Deepfakes, copying

Conclusion. Generative AI is a powerful assistant but not an authority, so its answers must be checked and used honestly.

Model answer D3: IoT, cloud and e-services in Nepal (10 marks)

Introduction. Three contemporary technologies connect people, machines and services: IoT, cloud computing and the e-services of government and business.

Internet of Things (IoT). IoT is a network of physical objects fitted with sensors, software and internet connection, which collect and exchange data without human help.

Its parts are the sensor (collects data), the network (Wi-Fi, mobile data), the cloud or server (stores and analyses) and the application (shows results or controls the device).

Uses: smart home, smart farming, smart meters, health bands, vehicle tracking, flood warning.

Cloud computing. It is the delivery of computing services such as storage, servers and software over the internet, paid for by use.

Service models: IaaS gives the raw servers (Amazon EC2), PaaS gives a platform to build apps (Google App Engine) and SaaS gives ready software (Gmail, Google Docs).

Advantages: low cost, access anywhere, easy scaling and automatic backup; limitations: needs the internet, and security and privacy depend on the provider.

Model You manage Example
IaaS Operating system and apps Virtual server
PaaS Your app only App platform
SaaS Nothing, just use Gmail

e-Services in Nepal.

  1. e-Commerce: buying and selling online, with Daraz, Sastodeal and food-delivery apps; payment by eSewa, Khalti, Fonepay and ConnectIPS.
  2. e-Governance: government services online, such as the Nagarik App, online passport and driving-licence applications, PAN registration and vehicle tax.
  3. e-Education: online classes, digital libraries, learning apps and results on the NEB website.

Benefits. Saves time and travel, reduces corruption through records, works 24 hours and reaches remote areas. Challenges: poor internet in rural places, low digital literacy, cyber-crime and electricity cuts.

Conclusion. IoT collects the data, the cloud stores and processes it, and e-services deliver the benefit to citizens, so together they build Digital Nepal.
